name: European Stag Beetle
range: Broadleaf woods, parks and gardens across Europe to the Caucasus and western Kazakhstan
tagline: Years underground, then a few weeks with antlers
lede: On a warm June evening, a big dark beetle lumbers through the air with a low buzz, its head crowned by what look like a pair of antlers. The European stag beetle spends years hidden underground as a grub in rotting wood, then has just a few weeks in the open to fight, mate and lay eggs.
home:
European stag beetles are found across much of Europe, though never in Ireland. They are widespread in southern Germany, in the hills of Hungary and Romania, and in northern and central Italy, but only in the northern half of Spain and Portugal. In Britain they are largely confined to the south-east of England. Beyond Europe they reach the Caucasus, Asia Minor, Syria and western Kazakhstan.

The beetle depends on dead and dying broadleaf trees, especially oak, along with lime, beech, willow, ash, black poplar, horse chestnut, wild cherry and walnut. It is now extinct in Latvia, and it vanished from Denmark around 1970 before being reintroduced in 2013. Croatia and Slovakia are the only countries where its range is currently growing.
anatomy:
This is the largest beetle in Europe. Males reach up to 7.5 centimetres long, while females measure 3 to 5 centimetres. Both are mostly black with reddish wing cases, and males also have red mandibles, hugely enlarged into the 'antlers' that give the species its name. Beetles from Spain, Germany and the Netherlands tend to be bigger than those from Belgium or Britain.

For all their menace, a male's mandibles are too weak to hurt a person, though a female can give a painful bite. The grub is soft, cream-coloured and almost see-through, curled into the shape of a letter C, with six orange legs, an orange head and sharp brown pincers. It is completely blind.
life:
Adults appear from late May to early August and are most active in the evening. They feed only on liquids, sipping nectar, tree sap and the juice of fallen fruit. Males take to the air more readily than females, with a slow, clumsy flight that makes a distinctive low-pitched hum, usually at dusk. In an ancient forest in northern Italy, radio-tracked males were mostly seen flying at sunset and resting on standing trees by day, while females stayed mainly underground near dead wood. Warm, humid weather suited the males' flights best, and the beetles were busiest in June, early in their short adult lives.

When something large approaches, a stag beetle's instinct is to freeze, which makes it an obliging subject for photographers. In Britain it is eaten by cats, foxes, badgers, crows, magpies, woodpeckers, kestrels and even false black widow spiders. Magpies have been seen waiting at an emergence site to pick off the beetles one by one and eat their abdomens. In Italy, the main predator is the hooded crow.
family:
Males use their great jaws to wrestle rivals for females, each trying to throw the other off a log or branch. A mated female then lays about 30 eggs in a piece of decaying wood deep in the soil.

The grubs eat rotting wood wherever they find it: tree stumps, old trees and shrubs, rotting fence posts, compost heaps and leaf mould. They moult through several stages over 3 to 7 years before turning into pupae. Work by the entomologist Charlie Morgan in the late 1970s showed that the pupa spends about 3 months in the soil before the adult emerges in summer. After all those years underground, the adult beetle lives only a few weeks.
remarkable: Stag beetle grubs talk to each other. Each has tiny combs on its legs, and by rubbing them it makes sounds that other grubs nearby can pick up, a form of signalling called stridulation, carried out in the dark inside rotting wood.
outlook:
The European stag beetle is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN. It is still widely distributed, but it is declining significantly in the north and centre of its range, and the future of Europe's forests puts it close to qualifying as Vulnerable. Its natural food, rotting wood below ground, is becoming scarcer.

It is protected under the European Union's Habitats Directive of 1992, which requires member states to set aside special areas of conservation for it. It is also listed under the Berne Convention of 1982 and on Schedule 5 of the UK's Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.
people:
Both the scientific and common names come from the likeness of the male's mandibles to a stag's antlers, and from the way males use them in combat, much as deer do. In Britain, female stag beetles are often confused with the lesser stag beetle, which is smaller, entirely black and has a larger, squarer head.

Gardeners and landowners can help by building log pyramids, also called stumperies: upright logs buried in the ground, which provide plenty of rotting broadleaf wood below the surface for the grubs to eat. Because the grubs also feed in compost heaps and old fence posts, the beetle can turn up in gardens as well as woods.
relatives:
The European stag beetle belongs to the stag beetle family, Lucanidae, and is the type example of its genus, Lucanus, which is divided into two subgenera. Carl Linnaeus described it in 1758, and four subspecies are now recognised, including L. c. turcicus and L. c. judaicus.

Its British look-alike, the lesser stag beetle, can also be told apart by its grubs: they feed on wood above ground, whereas those of the European stag beetle feed below it.
didYouKnow: Tiny mites hitch rides on stag beetles, clinging to the soft joint between the head and the thorax to travel from place to place.

choices: Around 20 years, inside a single oak stump
quiz.explanation: The grubs feed on rotting wood for 3 to 7 years before they pupate.

quiz.explanation: Males wrestle each other for females, trying to throw a rival off a log or branch.

choices: Hungary, apart from its lowland plains
quiz.explanation: It is widespread across Europe but has never been found in Ireland.

name: Bush Dog
range: Lowland forests and wet savannas from Costa Rica to northern Argentina
tagline: A stubby little wild dog that hunts in family packs
lede: Short-legged, stocky and reddish-brown, the bush dog looks more like an otter than a wolf. It hunts in close family packs through the forests of South America, and it is so rarely seen that the first scientist to find its bones thought it had died out long ago.
home:
Bush dogs range from Costa Rica in Central America through much of South America east of the Andes, as far south as central Bolivia, Paraguay and southern Brazil. Despite this huge range, they are very rare almost everywhere except Suriname, Guyana and Peru.

They live mainly in lowland forest up to about 1,900 metres, in wet savannas and in other habitats near rivers, though they also turn up in drier cerrado and open pasture. Packs shelter in hollow logs and cavities such as old armadillo burrows. Repeated sightings in Costa Rica's Talamanca Mountains, at elevations up to 2,119 metres, suggest they may be spreading north and uphill. Fossils from between 300 and 900 AD show they once lived on Trinidad too.
anatomy:
Adults have a head and body 57 to 75 centimetres long and a bushy tail of 12.5 to 15 centimetres. They stand just 20 to 30 centimetres at the shoulder and weigh 5 to 8 kg. The fur is soft, long and brownish-tan, with a lighter reddish tinge on the head, neck and back and darker underparts, sometimes with a pale throat patch. Young bush dogs are black all over. The legs are short, the snout is blunt and the ears are small.

Partially webbed toes make them efficient swimmers. Their teeth are built for meat: uniquely among American wild dogs they have 38 teeth, and they share with the dhole and the African wild dog a specialised lower molar with a single cusp that lengthens its cutting blade. Both sexes carry large scent glands at the rear.
life:
Bush dogs are carnivores that hunt by day, chiefly large rodents such as pacas, agoutis, acouchis and capybaras. When chasing a paca, part of the pack follows it on land while others wait in the water, where it often tries to escape. Packmates keep in touch with frequent whines, perhaps because they can see so little in the dense undergrowth.

A pack is a single breeding pair and their close relatives, roaming a home range of 3.8 to 10 square kilometres. Bush dogs seem to be the most sociable of South America's wild dogs. They mostly choose prey that is unlikely to hurt them, since a lone dog can break its canines tackling a paca, but together they can bring down peccaries and rheas. Their skulls cope well with pulling backwards, which fits reports of them hauling armadillos out of burrows.
family:
Bush dogs mate at any time of year. Only the adult pair breed, and the rest of the pack help to raise and guard the pups. After a pregnancy of 65 to 83 days the female gives birth to 3 to 6 pups, occasionally as many as 10. Newborns are blind and helpless and weigh 125 to 190 grams.

Their eyes open after 14 to 19 days, and soon afterwards they first venture out of the den. They are weaned at around four weeks and mature at one year. When the family feeds on a large carcass, the parents position themselves at either end, making it easier for the pups to tear it open. In captivity bush dogs can live for up to 10 years.
remarkable: For their size, bush dogs tackle astonishing prey. A pack of six was once seen hunting a South American tapir for 3 hours, biting at its legs until it collapsed, exhausted and badly wounded. That tapir weighed at least 21 times as much as one bush dog; by comparison, the elephants that lion prides sometimes kill are only 10 to 15 times heavier than a single lion.
outlook:
The bush dog is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN, after a population fall of roughly 20 to 25% over 12 years. The biggest threat is the loss of forest, especially Amazonian clear-cutting for timber, cattle and palm oil. Hunting by people also removes the dogs' prey, and diseases caught from domestic dogs are a growing worry as settlements push into their habitat.

Hunting bush dogs is illegal in most countries where they live, though Guyana and Suriname have no explicit ban and enforcement is often weak elsewhere. Because camera traps rarely catch them, researchers are trying scent-detection dogs to find their burrows. Protected areas such as the Yasuni Biosphere Reserve may hold stable populations.
people:
The palaeontologist Peter Wilhelm Lund first described the species from bones found in a Brazilian cave in 1839, and believed it was already extinct; living animals were only found later. It remains one of the least studied wild dogs in the world, shy and scattered thinly through dense habitat.

Its local names are colourful. In Brazil it is cachorro-vinagre, 'vinegar dog', or cachorro-do-mato, 'bush dog'. Spanish speakers call it perro vinagre, zorro vinagre ('vinegar fox'), perro de agua ('water dog') and perro de monte, 'woodland dog'. The first camera-trap photos in Argentina were taken only in 2016.
relatives:
The bush dog is the only living species in its genus, Speothos. Genetic evidence points to the maned wolf of central South America, or perhaps the African wild dog, as its closest living relative. With 74 chromosomes, it cannot produce fertile hybrids with other members of the dog family.

Three subspecies are recognised: the South American bush dog across most of Brazil and the Amazon basin, the Panamanian bush dog from Panama to western Ecuador, and the southern bush dog of southern Brazil, Paraguay and the far north-east of Argentina.
didYouKnow: A computer study of its skull found that the bush dog bites with half the force of a grey wolf, despite weighing at least 7 times less.

choices: Fruit and insects gathered on the forest floor

quiz.explanation: He described it from bones in a Brazilian cave; living animals were found later.

name: Lion's Mane Jellyfish
range: Cold waters of the Arctic, northern Atlantic and northern Pacific
tagline: A drifting giant with tentacles longer than a whale
lede: Trailing a curtain of tentacles that can stretch further than the length of a blue whale, the lion's mane is one of the largest jellyfish on Earth. It drifts alone through cold northern seas, a slowly pulsing bell of red and purple with a sting that summer swimmers learn to respect.
home:
Lion's mane jellyfish live in the cold, boreal waters of the Arctic and the northern Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. They are common in the English Channel, the Irish Sea and the North Sea, and in western Scandinavian waters south to the Kattegat and Øresund. In warmer spells some drift into the south-western Baltic, where the water is not salty enough for them to breed. Along the east coast of the United States they have long been seen in the larger bays south of 42°N.

Jellyfish that may be the same species also live in seas near Australia and New Zealand. Lion's manes stay very close to the surface, no deeper than 20 metres, and larger ones tend to live further offshore than smaller ones.
anatomy:
Most lion's manes in lower latitudes have a bell about 50 centimetres across, but in the far north they can exceed 2 metres. The largest on record, measured off Massachusetts in 1865, had a bell 210 centimetres wide and tentacles about 36.6 metres long, though some doubt whether that specimen really belonged to this species. Young jellyfish are light orange or tan, darkening with age.

Instead of a simple round bell, this species has one divided into eight lobes, like an eight-pointed star. Each lobe carries about 70 to 150 tentacles in four rows, around 1,200 in all, and they are described as extremely sticky. A balance organ called a rhopalium sits in each of the eight notches between lobes, helping the animal stay oriented, while broad, frilly oral arms packed with stinging cells hang from the central mouth.
life:
A lion's mane swims only weakly, its slow pulses nudging it forward, so it relies on ocean currents to travel long distances. Unlike most open-sea jellyfish, it lives a solitary life and rarely gathers in groups. It is most often seen in late summer and autumn, when it has grown large and currents begin to sweep it towards the shore.

Its tentacles catch fish, zooplankton and smaller jellyfish, which are pulled in to the mouth. Fully grown adults have few enemies, but young ones are eaten by seabirds, ocean sunfish, other jellyfish and most sea turtles, and anemones eat both young and adults. Around eastern Canada in summer, leatherback turtles feed almost entirely on lion's manes, eating them in large quantities.
family:
The lion's mane lives for about a year and passes through four stages. A female carries her fertilised eggs in a tentacle until they develop into larvae, then sets the larvae down on a hard surface, where each grows into a small polyp.

The polyps reproduce without mating, budding off stacks of tiny, immature jellyfish called ephyrae. These break away one by one and grow into the familiar adult medusa. So, like other jellyfish, the lion's mane reproduces sexually as an adult and asexually as a polyp.
remarkable: Its tentacles are so long that it ranks among the longest animals known. The television quiz show QI once named it the longest of all, before correcting itself in favour of a bootlace worm washed up at St Andrews in 1864 and said to exceed 55 metres. Since bootlace worms stretch easily, that record is doubted, and the jellyfish may yet deserve the title.
outlook:
No particular threats to the lion's mane are described, and it remains common around the coasts of northern Europe. Spells of warmer water already carry some individuals outside their usual waters, and the full picture is muddied because scientists still disagree about where its species boundaries lie.

For people, the concern runs the other way. The jellyfish's tentacles can keep stinging for up to 25 days after breaking off, which could harm any animal that touches them, including fish raised in sea farms where the jellyfish live.
people:
Its sting is very painful, like an intense itching or burning, and usually causes temporary pain and redness. Healthy people are not known to have died from it, and vinegar can disarm the stinging cells. Being stung over much of the body by a whole jellyfish, inner tentacles included, can have wider effects and needs medical care, and a severe sting in deep water can cause panic and drowning. In July 2010, about 150 people were stung at Wallis Sands State Beach in New Hampshire, probably by the fragments of a single broken-up jellyfish.

It is also known as the arctic red jellyfish, hair jelly, snottie, sea blubber and giant jellyfish. It is the culprit in Arthur Conan Doyle's 1926 Sherlock Holmes story 'The Adventure of the Lion's Mane', and a widely shared photograph of a giant one dwarfing a diver turned out to be a hoax.
relatives:
The lion's mane belongs to the genus Cyanea, whose classification is still debated; some zoologists suggest every species in it should be treated as one. In the eastern North Atlantic it lives alongside the blue jellyfish, Cyanea lamarckii, which is blue rather than red and much smaller, usually 10 to 20 centimetres across.

Populations around Japan are sometimes treated as a separate species or subspecies, Cyanea nozakii, and in 2015 Russian researchers announced a possible sister species, Cyanea tzetlinii, from the White Sea.
didYouKnow: Its common name comes from its showy mass of trailing tentacles, which reminded people of a lion's mane.

quiz.prompt: How many lobes does the lion's mane's bell have?
quiz.explanation: The bell is divided into eight lobes, like an eight-pointed star.

quiz.explanation: In summer, leatherbacks there feed almost entirely on them.

quiz.prompt: What can be used to deactivate its stinging cells?
choices: Sand rubbed firmly over the sting
quiz.explanation: Vinegar can be used to disarm the stinging cells.

name: Galápagos Tortoise
range: Seven of the Galápagos Islands, Ecuador
tagline: The giant tortoise that helped inspire Darwin
lede: The Galápagos tortoise is the largest tortoise alive, a reptile weighing as much as 417 kg that can outlive the people who meet it. Its islands are even named after it, and the way its shell changes from one island to the next helped set Charles Darwin thinking about evolution.
home:
Galápagos tortoises are native to seven of the Galápagos Islands, in the Pacific Ocean off Ecuador. Five populations live on the volcanoes of Isabela, the largest island, and others on islands such as Santa Cruz, San Cristóbal, Española, Pinzón and Santiago. On the bigger, wetter islands they migrate with the seasons, between low plains that turn grassy in the wet season and higher meadows, up to about 610 metres, in the dry season. They have followed the same routes for generations, wearing paths through the undergrowth known as 'tortoise highways'.

They rest in mud wallows and rain pools, take dust baths against parasites, and may sleep in a snug hollow in the earth called a pallet.
anatomy:
Big males weigh 272 to 317 kg and females 136 to 181 kg, and the largest individuals have reached 1.87 metres long. Size varies hugely, though: tortoises on Pinzón reach only about 76 kg. The dull brown or grey shell is fused to the ribs, and lichens sometimes grow on it. The legs are thick and stumpy, with five claws on the front feet and four on the back.

Shell shape depends on the island. Where humid highlands keep plenty of plants near the ground, as on Santa Cruz, tortoises are larger, with domed shells and short necks. On small, dry islands like Española and Pinzón they are smaller, with 'saddleback' shells arched up at the front and long necks and legs, which help them reach tall prickly pear cactus. When a saddleback pulls in its head, a gap remains over its neck, a sign that its ancestors had no predators to fear.
life:
Being cold-blooded, a tortoise basks for 1 to 2 hours after dawn, then forages for 8 to 9 hours, walking at about 0.3 km/h. It eats cacti, grasses, leaves, lichens and berries, and even the fruit of the poison apple tree. Most of its water comes from dew and juicy plants, especially Opuntia cactus, so it can go more than six months without drinking. On dry islands, generations of tortoises licking dew from boulders have worn hollows into the rock.

Finches and mockingbirds pick parasites off their skin. A tortoise signals that it is ready by rising up and stretching out its neck and legs. Occasionally a tortoise has been seen to drop flat on a bird that ventured underneath, then eat it.
family:
Mating can happen year-round, peaking between February and June. Rival males rise up on their legs, stretch their necks and gape, and the shorter one usually backs down. During mating the male makes hoarse, rhythmic groans, one of the few sounds a tortoise makes. From July to November, females walk several kilometres to dry, sandy nesting areas, dig a 30 centimetre hole with their hind legs, and lay up to 16 eggs the size of billiard balls. Nest temperature decides the sex: cooler nests produce more males, warmer ones more females.

Hatchlings emerge after four to eight months, weighing just 50 grams. They mature at 20 to 25 years in captivity, perhaps 40 in the wild, and wild tortoises are thought to live more than 100 years. Harriet, at Australia Zoo, died in 2006 at an estimated age of over 170.
remarkable: Darwin's five-week visit in 1835 made this tortoise famous. The islands' vice-governor told him he could tell which island any tortoise came from by its shell. Darwin later reasoned that animals on separate islands might become different if kept apart long enough, a key step towards his theory. Yet the 30 adult tortoises taken aboard the Beagle were eaten on the voyage and their shells thrown overboard.
outlook:
Tortoise numbers fell from around 250,000 in the 16th century to just 3,060 in a 1974 census, as sailors, whalers and settlers took them for meat and oil, cleared land and brought rats, goats, pigs, dogs and cats. The Floreana subspecies was gone by about 1850, and Lonesome George, the last Pinta tortoise, died in 2012. All surviving subspecies are classed by the IUCN as Vulnerable or worse.

Breeding programmes since 1965 have reversed much of this. On Española only 14 adults remained, and their descendants, hundreds of them fathered by a male called Diego, now number over 1,000. Rats have been cleared from Pinzón, more than 41,000 goats were removed from Pinta, and the total has climbed back above 19,000.
people:
Spanish explorers who reached the islands in 1535 named them after the tortoises, from the Spanish galápago, meaning tortoise. Their discoverer, Bishop Tomás de Berlanga, wrote that each could carry a man on its back. Later sailors prized them because they could survive aboard ship for a year or more without food or water, providing fresh meat, while the water stored in their bodies could be drunk. Pirates and naval captains such as William Dampier and David Porter praised the taste.

Darwin himself rode them, rapping on the back of their shells to make them walk, and found it very hard to keep his balance.
relatives:
All Galápagos tortoises descend from ancestors that drifted about 1,000 km from mainland South America, probably carried by the Humboldt Current; tortoises float and can survive months without food or fresh water. Their closest living relative is the much smaller Chaco tortoise of Argentina and Paraguay. The oldest islands, Española and San Cristóbal, were colonised first, and tortoises then spread island by island.

Since 2021 the populations are usually treated as 15 subspecies of a single species, 12 still living. The only other surviving group of island giant tortoises is the Aldabra giant tortoise of the Indian Ocean.
didYouKnow: Newly hatched tortoises may take several weeks to dig up to the surface, surviving on their yolk sac for up to seven months.

name: Burrowing Owl
range: Open grasslands and deserts from southern Canada to Tierra del Fuego
tagline: A long-legged owl that lives underground
lede: Standing on stilt-like legs at the entrance to a hole in the ground, the burrowing owl looks like an owl that took a wrong turn. Rather than roosting in trees, it makes its home below the surface of open grassland and desert, and it is often out and about in broad daylight.
home:
Burrowing owls live in open, dry country with low vegetation: grasslands, rangelands, farmland, deserts, badlands and chaparral. They range from the southern parts of western Canada through the western United States and Mexico to western Panama, across Florida and some Caribbean islands, and through every country of South America, avoiding only the dense Amazon interior and the highest Andes. South of the Amazon they are widespread from southern Brazil and the Pantanal to Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego.

Most are resident year-round, but birds breeding in Canada and the northern United States migrate to Mexico and the southern US in winter. They also adapt to airports, golf courses, farms and city parks.
anatomy:
A burrowing owl is 19 to 28 centimetres long, with a wingspan of 50.8 to 61 centimetres, and weighs 140 to 240 grams, a little bigger than an American robin. It has no ear tufts, a flattened facial disc, bright eyes, bold white eyebrows and a white chin patch that it puffs out when it bobs its head in agitation. Adults are brown above with white spots, and white below with brown spots or bars.

Its greyish legs are longer than those of other owls, which lets it sprint after prey on the ground. Females tend to be heavier, but males look paler, because they spend more time outside the burrow in daylight and their feathers become bleached by the sun.
life:
Burrowing owls avoid the midday heat and do most of their hunting around dawn and dusk. They watch from a perch and swoop down, catch insects in flight, or chase prey on foot. Roughly two thirds of the diet is small vertebrates and one third invertebrates, mainly big insects and small rodents. They are especially fond of termites, crickets, grasshoppers and certain scarab beetles, and they also take lizards, frogs, small birds and even bats. Unusually for owls, they eat fruit, especially from cholla and prickly pear cacti.

They usually fly only in short, low bursts. Their enemies include badgers, coyotes, snakes, cats and dogs, and many are killed by traffic while crossing roads.
family:
Nesting begins in late March or April in North America. Most birds have one mate, and pairs sometimes nest in loose colonies. They line the nest with all sorts of materials, most often cattle dung, which probably helps to control the microclimate inside the burrow. The female lays 4 to 12 eggs, usually 9, one every day or two, and incubates them for 3 to 4 weeks while the male brings her food.

Both parents feed the chicks, which make short flights about four weeks after hatching and are still fed for another 1 to 3 months. Burrowing owls live at least 9 years in the wild and over 10 in captivity.
remarkable: When threatened inside its burrow, the owl makes rattling and hissing sounds much like a rattlesnake, which often uses the same ground squirrel burrows. This seems to be acoustic mimicry, and it works well against animals that have learned to fear rattlesnakes.
outlook:
The burrowing owl is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, because it is common in open country across much of Latin America and is even spreading as the edges of the Amazon are deforested. In North America it is in trouble: it is endangered in Canada, threatened in Mexico, and listed as threatened in Colorado and Florida. In 2024 conservation groups petitioned for endangered or threatened status for five California populations.

The main problems are habitat loss and campaigns to kill prairie dogs and ground squirrels, whose burrows most owls depend on. Fewer burrows crowd owls together and make them easier for predators to find. Where development threatens a colony, owls can be coaxed to a prepared site nearby, using one-way doors over their old burrows.
people:
The owl was described in 1782 by the Spanish naturalist Juan Ignacio Molina from a specimen collected in Chile. Its species name, cunicularia, comes from the Latin for 'burrower' or 'miner', though the owls rarely dig their own homes. Instead they take over holes made by badgers, foxes, ground squirrels and prairie dogs, and only excavate where the soil is soft and none are available.

They tolerate people surprisingly well, nesting beside roads, farms, homes and irrigation canals, and they accept artificial plastic burrows. Urban owls have even taken to digging their own burrows, and they react differently to people and dogs than their rural cousins.
relatives:
The burrowing owl is now placed in Athene, the genus of the little owls, as a ground-dwelling member of that group, although some authorities have given it a genus of its own, Speotyto. There are 18 recognised subspecies, many in the Andes and the Caribbean, and two of these, on Antigua and Guadeloupe, died out around 1890 to 1905.

Fossils of similar owls from other Caribbean islands, including Jamaica and Puerto Rico, date to the end of the last ice age, when they probably vanished because of changes in climate and sea level.
didYouKnow: Burrowing owls scatter the droppings of large grazing animals around their burrow entrances to lure dung beetles, giving themselves a steady supply of food.

quiz.prompt: Where do burrowing owls usually get their burrows?
choices: From abandoned woodpecker holes in tall cactus
quiz.explanation: They mostly take over holes dug by prairie dogs, ground squirrels, badgers and foxes.

quiz.prompt: What sound does a threatened burrowing owl imitate?
choices: A barking prairie dog warning its colony
quiz.explanation: Its rattling hiss sounds like a rattlesnake, which deters many predators.

quiz.prompt: What do burrowing owls eat that most owls don't?
quiz.explanation: Unlike other owls, they eat fruit, especially from prickly pear and cholla cacti.

name: Cookiecutter Shark
range: Warm open oceans worldwide, especially between 20°N and 20°S
tagline: A glowing little shark that bites round holes in whales
lede: The cookiecutter shark is no longer than a forearm, yet it takes bites out of whales, great white sharks and even navy submarines. Its victims are left with perfectly round wounds, as if they had been stamped by a cookie cutter.
home:
This small shark lives in warm, open oceans worldwide, most commonly between 20°N and 20°S, where surface water is 18 to 26 °C. It has been recorded off the Bahamas, Brazil, West Africa, South Africa, Mauritius, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Fiji and Hawaii, and east to the Galápagos and Easter Island. It is often found near islands, perhaps to breed or because large prey gathers there.

Every day it migrates up and down by as much as 3 km each way. It spends daylight hours 1 to 3.7 km deep, then rises at night into the upper ocean, usually staying below 85 metres and only rarely reaching the surface.
anatomy:
Males reach 42 centimetres and females 56 centimetres. The body is cigar-shaped and chocolate brown, with a short, rounded snout, large green eyes, two tiny dorsal fins set far back and a broad tail fin. Around its throat runs a dark collar.

The mouth is ringed with fleshy, sucker-like lips. Its upper teeth are small and narrow, but the lower ones are large, knife-like and interlocked into a single saw-edged blade. A huge oily liver, up to about 35% of its weight, keeps it neutrally buoyant so it can hover with little effort, and heavily calcified cartilage in its skull and lips gives it a very strong bite.
life:
Hovering in the water column with small fins and weak muscles, the cookiecutter is an ambush hunter. Almost any medium or large ocean animal sharing its waters may be bitten: dolphins, porpoises, sperm and baleen whales, seals, dugongs, tunas, billfish, and sharks including blue, megamouth and great white sharks. It seals itself onto the victim with its lips and suction from its tongue, sinks in its teeth, then twists its body to cut out a plug about 5 centimetres across and 7 centimetres deep. Off Hawaii nearly every adult spinner dolphin carries its scars.

It also swallows smaller prey whole, including squid as long as itself, bristlemouths and copepods. These sharks sometimes travel in schools.
family:
Like other dogfish sharks, the cookiecutter gives birth to live young that are nourished by yolk inside the mother. Females have two working uteri and produce litters of 6 to 12 pups. The embryos seem to absorb their yolk slowly, suggesting a long pregnancy.

Newborns are 14 to 15 centimetres long. Males mature at about 36 centimetres and females at about 39 centimetres. Like all sharks it replaces its teeth, but it sheds whole rows of lower teeth at once and swallows them, recycling the calcium. One shark was calculated to have lost 15 sets, some 435 to 465 teeth, while growing from 14 to 50 centimetres.
remarkable: Its underside is covered with tiny light organs that give off a green glow, the strongest of any shark, which can last three hours after it is taken from the water. This glow matches light from above and hides its silhouette, except for the dark collar. Seen from below, the collar may look like a small fish, luring predators close enough to be bitten. If so, it would be the only known case where an absence of light attracts prey.
outlook:
The IUCN lists the cookiecutter shark as Least Concern. It is spread across the world's oceans, has no commercial value and is not especially vulnerable to fishing, turning up only now and then as bycatch on longlines and in trawls and plankton nets. New Zealand classes it as Not Threatened.

Its bites on fish and fishing nets may cause minor losses for commercial fisheries, but the species itself faces no significant threats.
people:
For centuries the round wounds puzzled people. An ancient Samoan legend said skipjack tuna entering Palauli Bay left pieces of their flesh as an offering to the chief, and later explanations blamed lampreys, bacteria or parasites. Only in 1971 did Everet Jones of the US fisheries service identify the culprit, and the shark expert Stewart Springer popularised the name cookiecutter, though he first called them 'demon whale-biters'.

In the 1970s and 1980s, cookiecutters bit holes in the rubber sonar domes and cables of US Navy submarines, forcing some back to base until fibreglass covers solved the problem. They have also damaged undersea cables, and a handful of long-distance swimmers, mostly in Hawaiian channels, have been bitten.
relatives:
The cookiecutter is a small squaliform shark in the family Dalatiidae, related to the dogfish sharks. The French naturalists Quoy and Gaimard described it from a specimen caught off Brazil during an 1817 to 1820 voyage, hence the species name brasiliensis. In 1865 Theodore Gill gave it its own genus, Isistius, after Isis, the Egyptian goddess of light.

Compared with its close relatives in the genera Euprotomicrus and Squaliolus, it has a denser skeleton and a larger, oilier liver, and it may cope better with water low in oxygen.
didYouKnow: Unlike other sharks, its retina has its sensing cells concentrated in a ring rather than a horizontal streak, which may help it focus on prey straight ahead.

quiz.prompt: Why did some US Navy submarines return to base in the 1970s?
choices: Shark bites on their sonar domes
Whales colliding with them during deep dives
quiz.explanation: Cookiecutters bit the rubber sonar domes, letting oil leak out.

quiz.prompt: What colour does the cookiecutter shark glow?
quiz.explanation: Its light organs give off a vivid green glow, the strongest of any shark.

quiz.prompt: What does the shark do with its old lower teeth?
choices: Grinds them against rocks to sharpen new ones
quiz.explanation: It swallows whole rows of shed teeth, recycling the calcium.

name: Menelaus Blue Morpho
range: Tropical forests from Mexico through Central and South America
tagline: A flash of blue made from light, not paint
lede: When a Menelaus blue morpho flaps lazily through a forest clearing, its wings flash an electric blue that seems almost to glow. That colour comes from microscopic structures on its scales that play tricks with light, and when the wings close, the butterfly turns a plain brown.
home:
The Menelaus blue morpho is a butterfly of the Neotropics, found from Mexico through Central America to South America, including Venezuela and the Cerrado, Brazil's vast tropical savanna. It is one of six morpho species in Costa Rica. It needs old-growth forest with a clear difference between understorey and canopy, and it struggles in the dry north Pacific region of Costa Rica, which is too arid for it.

Its ancestors may have lived in the Andes. Adults fly along rivers and wherever open land has been cleared, and they shelter from rain in small, enclosed spaces.
anatomy:
The wingspan is about 12 centimetres. Seen from above, the forewings and hindwings are a bright, iridescent blue edged with black, while the undersides are brown, with an eyespot 6.8 millimetres across. Females are more camouflaged on top than the vivid blue males, but the two sexes have the same forewing length and shape.

Each wing is covered in layered scales. In males, an outer layer of long, narrow cover scales lies over a layer of ground scales, whose ridges are built from stacked layers of chitin and air spaced about 80 nanometres apart. Because these structures are similar in size to the wavelength of light, they reflect blue strongly, and the colour shifts as the viewing angle changes.
life:
Both sexes have a slow, floppy flight and feed on rotting fruit that has fallen to the ground. Males usually patrol open clearings or fly high in the canopy, while females keep to the understorey, perching on tree stumps, and rise to the treetops only when it is time to lay eggs.

In the Cerrado, adults emerge together at the beginning and the end of the wet season, but not in the middle, when heavy rain can damage their wings. Their timing follows the food supply: the ripening of fruits spread by animals is one of the best predictors of when they appear.
family:
A female lays around 12 eggs, in clusters of 5 or 6, on the undersides of leaves, so the caterpillars can feed as soon as they hatch. The eggs are small, round and slightly flattened, pale green or whitish, and shaped like dew drops.

The caterpillars are social, red-brown with bright green spots, and covered in bristles that release an irritant when touched. They feed on plants such as Erythroxylum, Dalbergia and other legumes, preferring tender new leaves. Caterpillar numbers peak in the dry season, and they can pause their development to survive the drought, though many are eaten by predators as it drags on. The whole life cycle takes about 115 days, and the adult lives for just 3 to 4 weeks.
remarkable: Its wings repel water. Drops roll off as tiny beads, carrying dirt and dust with them, so the wings clean themselves. Along with being light, sturdy, heat-regulating and brilliantly coloured, this self-cleaning surface has drawn bioengineers hoping to copy the wing's nanostructures for colour-producing devices and gas sensors.
outlook:
Its striking colour has made the Menelaus blue morpho a target. During the 20th century it was widely hunted for collectors, and it is still widely caught or bred for decoration.

Because it depends on old-growth forest with a well-defined understorey and canopy, and cannot cope with very dry conditions, it is sensitive to changes in its forest home. Its emergence is tied to fruit supplies that in turn depend on the climate.
people:
The Menelaus blue morpho is one of the most familiar and recognisable insects of the American tropics. Over the past century, large numbers have built up in private and museum collections, prized by collectors, artists and designers. So many have been bred and traded that collectors disagree widely about how morphos should be classified, and museum specimens often have mismatched or missing abdomens, which hampers research.

Scientists study its wings with scanning electron microscopes and spectroscopy to understand exactly how they produce colour, and have found that 'Christmas-tree' shaped structures in the scales are what bend the light into its shimmering blue.
relatives:
It belongs to the genus Morpho, found from Mexico through South America except Chile, within the subfamily Morphinae. Older studies recognised 75 morpho species, newer ones about 30. The genus splits into groups that differ in flight style and in which forest layer they use, and this separation between understorey and canopy may have driven their diversification.

The Menelaus blue morpho is part of the achilles group, related to M. helenor and M. sulkowskyi. Its split from M. amathonte is thought to date to the Pliocene.
didYouKnow: Eyespots like the morpho's are thought to steer a predator's attack away from the body and towards the wing, and bigger ones can put predators off altogether.

quiz.prompt: What makes the morpho's wings blue?
choices: Blue blood in its wing veins
Pollen dust collected from forest flowers
quiz.explanation: Layers of chitin and air in the scales reflect blue light.

quiz.prompt: What do adult Menelaus blue morphos eat?
choices: Leaves of the plants they lay their eggs on
quiz.explanation: Both sexes feed on fruit that has fallen to the forest floor.

quiz.prompt: Why don't adults emerge in the middle of the wet season?
choices: Heavy rain can damage their wings
quiz.explanation: In the Cerrado they emerge at the start and end of the wet season instead.

name: Clouded Leopard
range: Dense forests from the Himalayan foothills to Southeast Asia and southern China
tagline: A tree-climbing cat with sabre-like fangs
lede: With the largest canine teeth for its size of any cat, the clouded leopard has been called a modern-day sabre-tooth. Its coat is marked with great dusky patches like storm clouds, ideal camouflage in the dim forests of southern Asia.
home:
Clouded leopards live in dense forests from the Himalayan foothills of Nepal, Bhutan and India through Myanmar, south-eastern Bangladesh, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Peninsular Malaysia to southern China, south of the Yangtze. They were found in Nepal in 1987 after being presumed extinct there, and have since been recorded as high as 3,498 metres in Langtang National Park.

They use habitats from semi-evergreen forest just 144 metres above sea level in India to forests above 3,700 metres in Sikkim, and in Thailand they live in both open, dry forest and closed forest. They are locally extinct in Singapore and Taiwan, where the last confirmed sign was a skin found in 1989.
anatomy:
This mid-sized cat weighs 11.5 to 23 kg. Males have a head and body of 81 to 108 centimetres and females 68.6 to 94 centimetres, and the tail adds another 61 to 91 centimetres and is used for balance in trees. The coat is grey or ochre, with dark blotches edged behind by curved black stripes, spots on the head and legs, and black ears.

Its legs are short and stout, with broad paws, and the hind legs are longer than the front ones for leaping. The bones of the forearm are not fused, giving extra freedom of movement for climbing. The upper canines measure 4 centimetres or more, about three times the width of their sockets. It can purr, and its pupils narrow to vertical slits.
life:
Clouded leopards are solitary. They rest in trees by day and hunt mainly at night on the forest floor, with peaks of activity around dusk and dawn, and they can jump more than 1.2 metres high. They stalk their prey or lie in wait, and after feeding they often retreat into the trees to digest and rest. Prey includes pig-tailed macaques, hog deer, porcupines, pangolins, ground squirrels, slow lorises, barking deer and pheasants, and one male in Malaysia was photographed carrying a binturong.

In Thailand, home ranges of radio-collared animals covered about 23 to 49 square kilometres. Their calls include a short, high meow, a loud crying call, a friendly snort known as prusten, low growls and hisses.
family:
Both sexes first breed at around 26 months. In the wild, mating usually takes place between December and March, and males can be very aggressive during courtship. Females can have one litter a year and raise the cubs alone.

After a pregnancy of about 93 days, the female gives birth to 1 to 5 cubs, usually 3, each weighing 140 to 280 grams. Their eyes open after about 10 days, and at first their spots are solid dark rather than ringed. They are active by five weeks, weaned at about three months, and independent at around 10 months. In captivity clouded leopards live on average 11 years, and one reached almost 17.
remarkable: It is one of the most talented climbers in the cat family. Captive clouded leopards climb down vertical tree trunks head first, and they can twist their feet to hang beneath a branch using only their bent hind paws and tail.
outlook:
The clouded leopard has been listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 2008. Fewer than 10,000 adults are thought to survive, with no more than 1,000 in any one population, and numbers are falling. It needs large areas of intact forest, which deforestation is removing, and it is poached for its skin and bones. In Myanmar, parts of at least 279 clouded leopards were seen in four markets between 1991 and 2006.

It is listed on CITES Appendix I and hunting is banned across most of its range, but enforcement is weak in some countries. Coordinated zoo breeding programmes began in the 1980s, though early attempts failed until keepers learned to introduce pairs young so they could bond.
people:
The species was first described in 1821 from the skin of an animal brought alive from Guangdong in China to the menagerie at the Exeter Exchange in London. It has been kept in zoos since the early 20th century, and International Clouded Leopard Day has been celebrated on 4 August since 2018.

The clouded leopard is the state animal of the Indian state of Meghalaya, and in the 1970s a print of Rama Samaraweera's painting of one was a best-seller in the United States. Its body parts are still sold for decoration and clothing in some markets, despite legal protection.
relatives:
The clouded leopard is the sister to all the other members of the big cat subfamily, Pantherinae, having split from them between 9.32 and 4.47 million years ago, and its skull was once seen as a link between the big cats and the small cats. Its closest relative is the Sunda clouded leopard of Borneo and Sumatra, recognised as a separate species only in 2006.

The two diverged between 2 and 0.93 million years ago, after clouded leopards reached the islands over a land bridge that is now under the sea.
didYouKnow: In one Thai forest, camera traps found clouded leopards were less common at the disturbed forest edge than in the quieter core.

quiz.prompt: Why is the clouded leopard called a modern-day sabre-tooth?
choices: It has the largest canines for its size
It kills deer much larger than itself by stabbing them
quiz.explanation: Its canines are the largest of any cat in proportion to its body.

quiz.prompt: Where does a clouded leopard usually rest during the day?
choices: In bamboo thickets beside mountain streams
quiz.explanation: It rests in trees by day and hunts on the forest floor at night.

quiz.prompt: When do clouded leopard cubs become independent?
choices: At 3 years, after their second winter
quiz.explanation: Cubs are weaned at about three months and leave at around 10 months.

name: Portuguese Man o' War
range: Surface waters of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans
tagline: A floating colony that sails the sea on a gas bubble
lede: It looks like a jellyfish, but the Portuguese man o' war is something stranger: a colony of many small units working together as one animal. It sails the ocean surface on a gas-filled float, trailing venomous tentacles as long as 30 metres beneath it.
home:
The Portuguese man o' war lives in the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans, floating at the very surface as part of the neuston, the community of organisms that live where sea meets air. Life there means intense ultraviolet light, the risk of drying out and rough seas. It cannot swim, so it goes wherever wind, currents and tides take it, sometimes travelling thousands of kilometres. Winds can drive large numbers into bays and onto beaches.

One mass stranding in the Bay of Biscay was traced back by computer modelling to the North Atlantic subtropical gyre, and the largest stranding on Ireland's coast in over 150 years has been studied in the same way.
anatomy:
The float, or pneumatophore, can be over 30 centimetres long, 13 centimetres wide and 15 centimetres tall. It is filled mostly with air that seeps in from the atmosphere, but up to 13% of the gas is carbon monoxide made by the animal itself. If attacked at the surface, the float can be deflated so the colony briefly sinks. Below it hang clusters of specialised units called zooids, seven types in all, which hunt, digest and reproduce.

The tentacles are usually about 10 metres long but can exceed 30 metres. They bear tiny coiled stinging threads called nematocysts that inject venom on contact. The colony is lopsided, with its float set to the left or the right, so the animal sails at about 45° to one side of the wind.
life:
The man o' war is a carnivore. Its tentacles trap and paralyse small fish, molluscs, small crustaceans and zooplankton, then reel them up to digestive zooids, which surround the food and release enzymes. Groups can number more than 1,000, and in large blooms they compete with fish, disrupt food webs and reduce catches.

Few animals eat it. Loggerhead turtles do, their skin too thick for the stings, as do blue sea slugs, violet sea snails and ocean sunfish. Yellow jacks and other fish shelter among the tentacles, and the man-of-war fish lives right among them, nibbling tentacles while perhaps luring other fish in. Blanket octopuses, immune to the venom, tear off tentacles to use as weapons.
family:
Each man o' war colony is either male or female. Its reproductive zooids sit on branching structures that are thought to drop away from the colony during breeding, and they release sperm or eggs directly into the sea. Fertilisation has never been seen in the wild, so nobody knows at what depth it happens.

A fertilised egg grows into a larva that buds off new zooids as it develops. The float and a single early feeding zooid appear first, then more feeding and tentacle-bearing zooids follow. The young colony grows underwater until its float becomes buoyant enough to lift it to the surface. Whether it will be left- or right-handed is settled early, while it is still below the waves.
remarkable: Every zooid in a man o' war grows from the same fertilised egg and is genetically identical, yet the zooids are derived from the two basic body plans of jellyfish and their kin, polyps and medusae, which in other species are whole animals. They stay connected for life and act like organs in one body, so the man o' war is a single organism in how it lives but many individuals in how it develops.
outlook:
Scientists expect blooms of the man o' war to become more frequent as the climate changes, with knock-on effects for ocean wildlife and for fisheries where it lives. Coastal communities already suffer smaller catches and damaged fishing gear when large numbers arrive.

Its lopsided build may protect the species from disaster. Because the wind pushes left- and right-handed colonies in opposite directions, at most half of a population can be blown towards the coast at once.
people:
The name comes from the man-of-war, a sailing warship, and the animal's resemblance to a Portuguese caravel under full sail. It is also called the bluebottle. Its genus and species names, Physalia physalis, come from the Greek for 'bubble' or 'bladder'.

Its sting causes severe pain for 1 to 3 hours and whip-like red welts that last two or three days, and in very rare cases it can be fatal. In Australia it causes up to 10,000 stings each summer, mostly on the east coast, and a stranded man o' war can lead to a beach being closed. Vinegar is the recommended rinse, and soaking in water at 45 °C for 20 minutes eases the pain.
relatives:
The man o' war is a siphonophore, a kind of hydrozoan, not a true jellyfish. Carl Linnaeus first described it in his Systema Naturae as Holothuria physalis, and Lamarck moved it to Physalia in 1801. Its family, Physaliidae, belongs to the Cystonectae, the earliest group of siphonophores to branch off.

It has often been treated as the only species in its genus, but genetic studies suggest several. A 2025 study recognised at least four, including the smaller Physalia utriculus, which has a single long tentacle, and Physalia mikazuki was described from Japan the same year.
didYouKnow: Detached tentacles and dead specimens washed up on the shore can sting as painfully as living ones, and stay potent for hours or even days.

quiz.prompt: What is a Portuguese man o' war?
choices: A giant single-celled organism that floats on the surface
quiz.explanation: It is a siphonophore, made of many genetically identical zooids.

quiz.prompt: Which unusual gas does its float contain?
choices: Hydrogen made by bacteria living inside it
quiz.explanation: Up to 13% of the gas in the float is carbon monoxide the animal produces.

quiz.prompt: Which turtle commonly eats the man o' war?
choices: Olive ridley, during its mass nesting
quiz.explanation: The loggerhead's skin is too thick for the stings to get through.

name: Gila Monster
range: Deserts and scrub of the south-western United States and Sonora, Mexico
tagline: America's only venomous lizard, and a medical marvel
lede: Heavy, slow and patterned like a beaded bag, the Gila monster is the only venomous lizard native to the United States. It rarely threatens anyone who leaves it alone, yet its painful bite has earned it a fearsome reputation across the desert south-west.
home:
Gila monsters live in the south-western United States and the Mexican state of Sonora, across Arizona and parts of California, Nevada, Utah and New Mexico. They inhabit scrubland, succulent desert and oak woodland, avoiding open flats and grasslands. They need shelter with a suitable microclimate and enough humidity, using burrows, thickets and rocky crevices in places such as Navajo Sandstone and old lava flows.

They depend on water too, and can be seen lying in puddles after summer rain. The name comes from the Gila River Basin in Arizona and New Mexico, where they were once plentiful.
anatomy:
This is the largest native lizard in North America north of Mexico. Its body measures 26 to 36 centimetres from snout to vent, the largest reach 51 to 56 centimetres in total, and it typically weighs 550 to 800 grams. It is stout and heavy, with a massive head, small-looking eyes protected by a third eyelid, and a fat tail where it stores energy. Its forked tongue is black-blue.

The scales of the head, back and tail contain small round bones called osteoderms, giving its skin a beaded look; the genus name Heloderma means 'studded skin'. Adults are black with yellow to pink markings, colours that may warn predators off. Venom comes from glands in the lower jaw and flows along grooves in the teeth into a wound as the lizard chews.
life:
Gila monsters spend 90% of their lives underground. They are active mostly in the mornings of spring and early summer, moving shelter every 4 to 5 days, and later may come out on warm nights or after thunderstorms. In one Utah study they were active on only 10 days of a 90-day season. A slow metabolism lets them use less than half the energy expected for a lizard their size, and they store water in the bladder.

They hunt by smell, flicking the tongue to track young rabbits, mice, ground squirrels, small birds, snakes, lizards, frogs, insects, carrion and especially eggs. Young ones can swallow half their own weight in a meal, and three or four big meals in spring may fuel a whole season. They can climb trees, cacti and even rough walls. Coyotes, badgers and birds of prey hunt them.
family:
Gila monsters come out of their winter dormancy in early March and mature at 4 to 5 years old. Mating takes place in April and May; the male searches for a female's scent with his tongue, and if she is not interested she bites him and chases him away. Rival males wrestle, arching and twisting until one pins the other beneath him.

The female lays up to eight eggs, rarely more than six, from late May into June, and is left thin and exhausted. The eggs hatch near the end of October, and the young go straight into hibernation without surfacing. Hatchlings are about 17 centimetres long and weigh around 34 grams, and their colours change dramatically over their first 6 months.
remarkable: A protein in its venom, exendin-4, is 53% identical to GLP-1, a human gut hormone that helps control insulin. A synthetic version, exenatide, was approved in the United States in 2005 to treat type 2 diabetes, and it led to the class of GLP-1 drugs now used for diabetes and obesity. Unlike the human hormone, the lizard version lasts long enough in the body to work well as a medicine.
outlook:
The Gila monster is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN. The greatest danger is the destruction of its habitat for building and farming. Lizards moved out of the way of development, even 1.2 km, struggle back to where they were found within 2 months, exposing themselves to predators along the way, so educating people may work better than relocation.

In 1952 it became the first venomous animal to be given legal protection, and it is protected by state law in Arizona, yet people still sometimes kill it out of fear. The San Diego Zoo first bred Gila monsters in captivity in 1963.
people:
Old West pioneers believed the Gila monster had deadly breath, could spit venom or leap into the air, and even lacked an anus. In 1891 the Tombstone doctor George Goodfellow let one of his captive lizards bite him on purpose; he spent five days in bed but recovered fully, and argued that bites were rarely deadly. Bites are very painful and need emergency care, and one death has been confirmed since 1930, in Colorado in 2024.

Today the lizard is Utah's state reptile, since 2019, and the Vegas Golden Knights chose one named Chance as their mascot. It starred in the film The Giant Gila Monster, though that 'monster' was actually played by a Mexican beaded lizard.
relatives:
The Gila monster's closest living relatives are the beaded lizards: three species in Mexico and one in Guatemala. Together they form the family Helodermatidae, whose history goes back to the Cretaceous, and because they have changed so little they are sometimes called living fossils. Gila monster bone fragments have been found in Late Pleistocene deposits near Las Vegas.

The palaeontologist Edward Drinker Cope named the species suspectum because he suspected, from the grooves in its teeth, that it was venomous. Although it looks like the monitor lizards, it is placed in a separate family.
didYouKnow: When it gets too hot, a Gila monster can cool itself by up to 2 °C by letting moisture evaporate from its cloaca.

quiz.prompt: Where does the Gila monster's venom come from?
choices: Glands behind the eyes, as in rattlesnakes
quiz.explanation: Venom flows from lower-jaw glands along grooves in its teeth.

quiz.prompt: What kind of drug was developed from a protein in its venom?
choices: An antidote for rattlesnake bites used in hospitals
quiz.explanation: Exenatide, based on exendin-4, treats type 2 diabetes.

quiz.prompt: How much of its life does a Gila monster spend underground?
choices: Half, mostly during the winter months
quiz.explanation: It spends 90% of its life in burrows or rocky shelters.
